Minnesota property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • All property shall be valued at its market value. (Minn. Stat. 273.11; source)
  • Local board of appeal and equalization meetings must be held between April 1 and May 31 each year. (Minn. Stat. 274.01; source)
  • A person who fails to appear before the local board after notice of an assessment increase, or fails to apply for review, may not appear before the county board of appeal and equalization (with exceptions, e.g. no notice of market value at least five days before the local meeting). (Minn. Stat. 274.01; source)
  • A property tax petition to district court or Tax Court is served on the county auditor, and the petition and proof of service must be filed with the district court administrator on or before April 30 of the year the tax becomes payable. (Minn. Stat. 278.01 subd. 1; source)
  • If notice of a valuation, classification or exempt-status change is first given after February 28 of the year taxes are payable, the petitioner has 60 days from the mailing date of the notice to appeal. (Minn. Stat. 278.01 subd. 4; source)
  • Appeal of a commissioner of revenue order to Tax Court must be served and filed within 60 days after the notice date of the order; the Tax Court may extend up to 30 more days for cause. (Minn. Stat. 271.06; source)
  • Tax Court Small Claims Division appeal fee is $150. (Minn. Stat. 271.06; source)
  • Redemption period for lands sold to the state at a tax judgment sale is generally three years from the date of sale to the state. (Minn. Stat. 281.17(a); source)
  • Redemption is one year for lands in a targeted community (except homesteaded lands) and for qualified mixed municipal solid waste facilities. (Minn. Stat. 281.17(b),(c); source)

How is property valued and taxed in Minnesota?

Minnesota lists real property by its January 2 value, and assessors must look at a fifth of all parcels each year, which puts every parcel on a five year maximum cycle (Minn. Stat. 273.01). The yardstick is market value. Minn. Stat. 273.11 bars assessors from picking a lower standard because the number will support a tax, and from using a forced-sale price.

Every owner of record gets a mailed valuation notice at least ten days before the local appeal board convenes (Minn. Stat. 273.121). It states two years of market value and classification, the assessor's address, and the meeting dates for the local board and the county board. An owner who never receives it still owes the tax, since a missed notice does not undo the assessment.

What are the two Minnesota payment dates and the late charges?

A parcel taxed over $100 pays in halves, the first before May 16 and the second before October 16 (Minn. Stat. 279.01). Missing a due date adds two percent for homestead and four percent for nonhomestead property. If any balance remains once the next month begins, another two or four percent is added. After that, each month through December adds one percent, up to a ceiling of eight percent for homestead and 12 percent for nonhomestead.

  • A statement mailed after April 24 pushes the spring deadline out to 21 days past its postmark.
  • A bill of $100 or less is payable in one lump on the spring date.
  • The treasurer can accept an amount above or below the installment and credits it to the oldest balance first.
  • A payment postmarked within one business day after the deadline earns a one-time penalty waiver.
  • Farm homestead owners have until November 15 for the second half.

Each autumn the county also mails a proposed tax notice, between November 11 and November 24 (Minn. Stat. 275.065). It compares this year's tax with each taxing authority's proposal for next year and names the evening budget hearings, which cannot start before 6:00 p.m. or fall before November 25.

What steps lead to a lower Minnesota assessment?

There are three stages, and skipping the first can limit the second. Town and city boards sit sometime from April 1 through May 31 (Minn. Stat. 274.01), with posted and published notice ten days ahead. Any aggrieved owner can ask the board to review a value or class. Cuts are capped: all reductions together may not shave more than one percent off the assessor's total, and the board has no power to exempt a parcel or drop it from the rolls.

An owner who was warned of a proposed increase and then ignores the hearing, or who never asks for review at all, generally loses the right to go before the county board. The exception covers an owner who did not get notice of the market value five days or more ahead of the local session. Local boards have 20 days to wrap up unless the revenue commissioner allows longer.

The county board takes over in June. Under Minn. Stat. 274.14 it convenes after the second Friday, may use as many as ten meeting days, and cannot act after June 30 apart from allowed corrections. One day must stretch into the evening, with sessions running to 7:00 p.m. or later. The last stop is court. Under Minn. Stat. 278.01, an owner can petition district court or Tax Court by serving a copy on the county auditor and filing proof of service with the court administrator by April 30 of the payable year. A change notice that first reaches the owner after February 28 starts a 60 day window counted from the date it was mailed.

Which dates drive the Minnesota property tax year?

The table lists the fixed dates in the statutes. Exact board meeting days differ by town, city and county and appear on each owner's valuation notice, so treat the notice as the final word.

What happens to unpaid Minnesota property tax when a house is sold?

Before land moves on the county books, the auditor searches for delinquent taxes. Section Minn. Stat. 272.12 has the auditor certify any that exist and, after payment or if there are none, stamp the deed "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered." A recorder cannot take most deeds without that stamp, though probate distribution deeds, foreclosure certificates and a handful of other documents are treated separately.

Long-term nonpayment ends in a forfeiture sale. Land sold to the state after a tax judgment can be redeemed for three years, according to Minn. Stat. 281.17. The window shrinks to one year in a targeted community, with homesteads excluded, and for a qualifying municipal solid waste facility. Classification for this purpose comes from the assessment year behind the judgment.

Charges for street, sewer and similar projects follow another process. Minn. Stat. 429.061 has the council hold a hearing after mailing owners the proposed amount, the prepayment option and the interest rate. To keep an appeal alive, an owner must file a signed objection with the clerk before or during the hearing, then serve notice on the mayor or clerk within 30 days of adoption. The property tax petition in section 278.01 does not reach these assessments.

What relief programs lower a Minnesota property tax bill?

Several programs exist, and each needs its own application. Match the program to the problem: a high value, a thin income or a payment crunch.

  • Homestead status brings a value exclusion that begins at 40 percent for homes worth $95,000 or less (Minn. Stat. 273.13, subdivision 35).
  • The refund in Minn. Stat. 290A.04 reaches $3,310 at most and stops once household income hits $135,410.
  • Minn. Stat. 290B.03 lets qualifying owners at least 65 years old, with household income up to $96,000, postpone tax payments.
  • A written request to the county board under Minn. Stat. 375.192 can cut value, tax, penalty or interest, with limits on earlier years.
  • Guard and reserve members on federal active service get four extra months on homestead due dates when they attach their orders.

Whoever inherits or buys a house should confirm its classification first. A homeowner wrongly shown as nonhomestead can ask the county board to correct it through section 375.192.

More questions about Minnesota Property Tax Guide

What dates do Minnesota property tax installments fall on?

The spring half falls before May 16 and the fall half before October 16 on any bill over $100. Smaller bills are paid whole in spring. Late-mailed statements get 21 days from the postmark.

What is the penalty for paying Minnesota property tax late?

Homestead owners pay 2 percent at the deadline and nonhomestead owners 4 percent, doubled if the balance carries into the next month, and then 1 percent per month until December. Penalties top out at 8 and 12 percent.

Where do I start if my Minnesota valuation looks too high?

Begin with the town or city board in April or May, move to the county board in June if needed, and use a court petition as the last step, filed by April 30 of the payable year. Special assessments follow their own objection route.

Can I sell a Minnesota house that has delinquent property taxes?

Yes, after the back taxes are cleared. The auditor flags them when the deed arrives and withholds the recording stamp until payment. Phone the treasurer's office for a written payoff figure before closing.

What is the redemption window after a Minnesota tax judgment sale?

Three years after the sale to the state in most cases. Targeted community land other than homesteads, and certain solid waste disposal facilities, get one year.

Minnesota offers property tax relief for qualifying homeowners, and official sources explain the rules.

What the official sources say

  • Property not used as a homestead on the assessment date but used as a homestead on December 31 of a year is classified class 1 or 2a. (Minn. Stat. 273.124; source)
  • A taxpayer must notify the county assessor in writing by December 31 of the year of occupancy to qualify for homestead classification under that subdivision. (Minn. Stat. 273.124; source)
  • Minnesota DOR says a law change increased the 2025 Homestead Credit Refund for homeowners by nearly 15%. (Property Tax Refund | Minnesota Department of Revenue; source)

What does the Minnesota homestead exemption cover?

Minnesota uses the word homestead for two separate protections. One shields a home from most creditors under Chapter 510. The other is a property tax classification that the county assessor grants under Minn. Stat. 273.124, and it lowers the taxable value of the house. Anyone selling a Minnesota home usually meets both at the same closing table.

Section 510.01 protects the house a debtor owns and occupies as a dwelling, plus the land under it within stated limits, from seizure or sale for debts not charged against it in writing. The carve-outs in that same section are debts for work or materials that went into building, repairing or improving the homestead, and wages owed to laborers or servants.

How much of a Minnesota home is protected from creditors?

Under Minn. Stat. 510.02, a homestead may include up to 160 acres, and the exemption may not exceed $540,000 per homestead. If the homestead is used mainly for agriculture, the cap rises to $1,350,000. The statute also says these dollar figures are adjusted periodically and that the commissioner of commerce publishes the changes, so confirm the current figure before relying on any older number.

The exemption has edges. According to Minn. Stat. 510.05, it is not reduced by, and does not reach, the following:

  • a mortgage lawfully placed on the home;
  • a valid lien for taxes or assessments;
  • claims for state hospital care or medical assistance filed under sections 246.53 or 256B.15;
  • charges that arise under the laws on laborers' or material suppliers' liens.

Who qualifies for homestead classification and how do you apply?

Residential real estate occupied and used as a homestead by its owner, who must be a Minnesota resident, is a residential homestead under Minn. Stat. 273.124, subdivision 1. A person who meets that test must file a homestead application with the county assessor to get the classification the first time. The application must be signed by each owner who lives in the home and by each occupying owner's spouse.

The assessor also needs the Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number of each occupying owner, plus the name and number of that owner's spouse. Owners who leave the spouse's details off the form are treated as having chosen only partial homestead treatment, and the remainder of the house is classified as nonhomestead residential.

A relative of the owner can also make the house a homestead. The statute lists a parent, stepparent, child, stepchild, grandparent, grandchild, brother, sister, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece, by blood or marriage. The tax treatment then matches what the owner would receive if the owner lived there, and neither the owner nor the relative may claim a chapter 290A refund on that property.

What is the December 31 deadline for a newly bought Minnesota home?

A house that was not a homestead on the assessment date but was used as one on December 31 is class 1 or 2a for that year, and the taxpayer must notify the county assessor in writing by December 31 of the year of occupancy. This comes from subdivision 9 of Minn. Stat. 273.124. The assessor cannot deny full treatment to a property that was partly homesteaded on January 2 but fully occupied as a homestead on December 31.

If no homestead application is on file by December 31, the assessor classifies the property as nonhomestead for taxes payable the following year. The county assessor must publish a notice by December 1 each year reminding owners of that filing requirement.

  • File the homestead application with the county assessor, not the city clerk.
  • Have every occupying owner and spouse sign.
  • Send the written notice before December 31 if you moved in after the January 2 assessment date.

What does homestead status save on a Minnesota tax bill?

The saving comes through a market value exclusion in Minn. Stat. 273.13, subdivision 35. For a homestead valued at $95,000 or less, the exclusion is 40 percent of market value. Between $95,000 and $517,200, the exclusion is $38,000 minus nine percent of the value above $95,000. At $517,200 or more there is no exclusion.

Here is the arithmetic for a $200,000 home. The value above $95,000 is $105,000, and nine percent of that is $9,450. Subtract it from $38,000 and the exclusion is $28,550, so the taxable value starts from $171,450 before the classification rate is applied.

What happens to the homestead when you sell the house?

Homestead classification lasts until the property is sold or transferred, or until the owners, their spouses or the qualifying relatives stop using it as a homestead. Minn. Stat. 273.124 requires the owner to tell the assessor within 30 days of a sale, a transfer or a move-out. Missing that window carries a penalty and ends the homestead status.

The creditor protection follows the money for a limited time. Under Minn. Stat. 510.07, the owner may sell and convey the homestead without exposing the proceeds, for one year after the sale, to debts the homestead was exempt from. Court-ordered child support or maintenance in arrears is the exception. Insurance proceeds on an exempt homestead are exempt for one year as well.

An owner who moves out has a clock running. If the owner stops occupying the home for more than six consecutive months, the home is treated as abandoned unless the owner files a notice with the county recorder claiming it as the homestead. The exemption never continues more than five years after that filing unless the family actually lived there for part of the term.

At closing, whenever the price is above $3,000, the grantor, grantee or their agent files a certificate of value with the county auditor when the deed is presented for recording (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

Which Minnesota homeowners can claim a property tax refund or deferral?

The homestead credit refund in Minn. Stat. 290A.04 pays when property taxes exceed a set percentage of household income. The statute table starts at 1.0 percent of income for the lowest brackets and climbs to 2.5 percent in the highest. The maximum refund is $3,310 for household incomes up to $50,099 and steps down through the brackets, to $650 for incomes from $130,350 to $135,409. Households at $135,410 or more receive nothing.

Timing is set in Minn. Stat. 290A.07. Most claimants are paid after September 15 and before September 30. Owners of manufactured homes are paid after August 1 and before August 15, or 60 days after the application arrives, whichever is later.

Older owners have a separate option. The senior citizens' deferral in Minn. Stat. 290B.03 requires these conditions:

  • the owner is 65 or older, and in a married couple one spouse is at least 65 and the other at least 62;
  • household income for the year before the first application is $96,000 or less;
  • the home has been the owner's homestead for at least five years;
  • there are no state or federal tax liens or judgment liens on it;
  • debts secured by the property do not exceed 75 percent of the assessor's estimated market value.

What happens to a Minnesota homestead after the owner dies?

If there is a surviving spouse, Minn. Stat. 524.2-402 sends the homestead to the spouse when the decedent left no descendants. When descendants survive, the spouse holds it for life and the remainder goes to the descendants in equal shares by representation. With no spouse and no will covering it, the homestead descends like other real estate.

A homestead that passes to the spouse, the descendants or a trust for them alone is exempt from debts that were not valid charges on it at death, except the state hospital and medical assistance claims mentioned above. A homestead that passes to anyone else answers for administration expenses, funeral costs, last illness expenses, taxes and debts. A personal representative selling a homestead in which a spouse takes an interest needs the spouse's written consent, as Minn. Stat. 524.3-715 spells out in clause 23.

An owner who missed the filing and discovers the error later can ask the county board for relief. Minn. Stat. 375.192 lets the board reduce or abate value or taxes on written application, but for the two prior years only in cases of clerical error or hardship, and the assessor and county auditor must approve the application first.

More questions about Minnesota Homestead Exemption

How much is the Minnesota homestead exemption worth against creditors?

It is capped at $540,000 per homestead, or $1,350,000 if the property is used mainly for agriculture, on up to 160 acres. The commissioner of commerce publishes adjustments to those figures, so check the current amount. The cap never reaches mortgages, valid tax or assessment liens, or mechanics' lien charges.

Do I have to reapply for Minnesota homestead classification every year?

No. Once granted, the classification stays until the property is sold or transferred or the owners stop living there. The assessor can still ask at any time for a new application to confirm that the property qualifies, and a name change or transfer may trigger a fresh request.

How soon must I tell the assessor after I sell or move out of a Minnesota home?

Within 30 days. The statute attaches a penalty to missing that deadline, and the property loses its homestead status. Send the notice to the county assessor and keep proof of the date you sent it.

Can a relative living in my Minnesota house get homestead treatment?

Yes, to the extent the treatment would apply if the owner lived there. The owner must file a homestead application with the relative's details, and if a different relative moves in, the owner must notify the assessor within 30 days. Neither person can claim a property tax refund for that home.

Are my Minnesota sale proceeds safe from creditors after closing?

For one year after the sale, the proceeds are protected from debts the homestead was exempt from. Court-ordered child support or maintenance arrears are not protected. After that year, ordinary creditors can reach the money unless another exemption applies.

This guide covers what official sources say about Minnesota estate and inheritance tax.

What the official sources say

  • Minnesota DOR lists the estate tax filing requirement value of estate as $3,000,000 for years of death 2020-present. (Estate Tax Filing Requirement | Minnesota Department of Revenue; source)
  • Minnesota DOR describes estate tax as applying to the Minnesota assets of a decedent's estate, filed and paid by the executor or personal representative. (Estate Tax | Minnesota Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Minnesota?
We buy Minnesota houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Does Minnesota have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Minnesota has an estate tax and has no inheritance tax. The estate tax is charged on a decedent's assets before they pass to heirs, and Minn. Stat. 291.01 imposes it on the transfer of the estate. An inheritance tax would fall on what each heir receives, and the Department of Revenue says Minnesota's version was repealed starting in 1980.

The department does not issue inheritance waiver or clearance letters, so no such document exists to request before an inherited Minnesota house is listed. A beneficiary generally does not report an inheritance on an income tax return, although pre-tax money in IRA and annuity accounts can carry income tax. Details are on the department's estate tax versus inheritance tax page.

When must a Minnesota estate file a return?

A Minnesota estate must file a return when its total gross value is above $3,000,000 for a death in 2020 or later. The federal filing level is much higher, $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths, so an estate between the two figures files with Minnesota alone.

Source: Minnesota Department of Revenue, Estate Tax Filing Requirement. The same page shows a $2,000,000 qualified small business or farm property deduction for deaths from 2020 forward.

What rate does Minnesota charge on an estate?

For deaths in 2018 and later the Minnesota rate starts at 13 percent and climbs to 16 percent on the top slice of the taxable estate. The Department of Revenue's rate guide lists the same 13 percent low and 16 percent high, and tells filers to complete federal Form 706 and Minnesota Form M706 to compute the actual bill.

  • 13 percent on a Minnesota taxable estate up to $7,100,000.
  • 13.6 percent on the slice from $7,100,000 to $8,100,000, after a base of $923,000.
  • 14.4 and 15.2 percent on the next two $1,000,000 slices.
  • 16 percent above $10,100,000, after a base of $1,355,000.

Under Minn. Stat. 291.03 the result is then multiplied by the Minnesota gross estate divided by the federal gross estate. Real property counts as located in the state where the land sits (Minn. Stat. 291.005), so a house in Minnesota belongs in the Minnesota share even when the owner lived somewhere else.

When are the Minnesota return and payment due?

Form M706 and the payment are due nine months after the date of death. Minnesota grants an automatic six-month extension to file and no extension to pay, so the tax is still due at nine months even when the return is filed later.

  • A death in January puts the regular due date in October and the extended filing date in April.
  • A death in August moves those dates to May and November.
  • A death in December moves them to September and March.

An estate can ask to pay in installments only if the IRS has granted a payment extension under Internal Revenue Code section 6161 or 6166, the Minnesota tax is $5,000 or more, the executor writes to the department within nine months of death naming payment dates that match the federal ones, and the installments are equal. Interest is owed on whatever stays unpaid after the regular due date. See due dates and extensions and installment payments.

Can heirs sell an inherited Minnesota house before the estate tax is settled?

Yes, because the personal representative holds statutory power to sell estate property to cover the tax. Minn. Stat. 291.16 gives every executor, administrator, or trustee full power to sell inherited property to pay the estate tax in the same way the law lets them sell to pay a decedent's debts.

The same chapter puts weight on the representative. Under Minn. Stat. 291.12 the representative must deduct or collect the tax before completing a transfer, becomes personally liable up to the value of the property held if a known tax goes unpaid, and need not deliver property until the tax and interest are accounted for. Heirs should expect any tax to be accounted for before the representative distributes sale money.

When the department accepts a return as filed it sends a Minnesota Notification of Closed Estate letter to the personal representative. If a federal Form 706 was required, that letter waits for a copy of the federal closing letter or audit report. Ask the estate's attorney and the title company which of these papers they want before closing, and call Minnesota Revenue estate tax at 651-556-3075 (weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) with questions about the letter.

What does a Minnesota estate's personal representative have to file besides the estate tax return?

A personal representative also files the decedent's final income tax returns and, when the estate earns enough, an estate income tax return. The Department of Revenue lists these duties on its personal representative page.

  • The final Form M1 is due April 15 of the year after death, even when a spouse survives.
  • Form M2 is required for each year the estate is open in which gross income reaches $600 or a beneficiary is a nonresident alien.
  • The estate's tax year starts the day after death and can end on the last day of any month chosen, within one year of death.
  • Property taxes that come due while the estate is open are the representative's to pay. Minnesota law sets the first half before May 16 and the second half before October 16, with a 2 percent penalty on homestead property and 4 percent on non-homestead property when a half is late (Minn. Stat. 279.01).
  • A request for early audit on Form M22 cuts the department's assessment window on income returns to 18 months from the usual 3.5 years, and does not apply to Form M706.

Federal and state law also make the representative liable for income and estate taxes if funds are distributed without keeping enough to pay them.

Do a family farm or small business get an estate tax break in Minnesota?

They can, through a deduction of up to $2,000,000 for qualified small business or farm property when the date of death is after December 31, 2022. The property must pass to a qualified family heir, and the executor claims the deduction on Schedule M706Q with the return.

Qualified small business property needs gross annual sales of $10,000,000 or less, material participation by the decedent or spouse, and three years of continuous ownership. Qualified farm property must be agricultural land classified class 2a and an agricultural homestead in the year of death.

The break has a three-year string attached. If the heir sells to a non-family buyer or a family member stops running the business or keeps the 2a classification within three years of the death, a recapture tax of 16 percent of the claimed exclusion comes due six months after that event (Minn. Stat. 291.03, subd. 11). The statute carves out a farm residence, garage, and the surrounding acre that is reclassified as class 4bb, when the heir has not substantially altered it. Informational returns are due 36 to 39 months after the death. More is on the deduction page.

More questions about Minnesota Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Minnesota tax the money or house I inherit?

No. Minnesota repealed its inheritance tax starting in 1980, and the Department of Revenue says it issues no inheritance waiver letters. The estate tax is charged to the estate before distribution. Pre-tax IRA and annuity money can still carry income tax.

What is the Minnesota estate tax rate?

The rate runs from 13 percent to 16 percent for deaths in 2018 and later. It is 13 percent on a Minnesota taxable estate up to $7,100,000 and reaches 16 percent above $10,100,000, then scaled by the Minnesota share of the federal gross estate under Minn. Stat. 291.03.

How soon after a death is Form M706 due?

Nine months after the date of death. A six-month extension to file is automatic, but there is no extension to pay, so the tax is still owed at nine months. Installments are possible only under the narrow conditions on the Department of Revenue's installment page.

Is an estate under $3,000,000 required to file a Minnesota estate tax return?

No. For deaths from 2020 forward the state requires a return only when the total gross value of the estate is above $3,000,000. A smaller estate can still owe the decedent's final income tax return and, if it earns $600 or more of gross income, an estate income tax return.

Who can answer questions about a Minnesota estate tax bill?

Minnesota Revenue's estate tax staff at 651-556-3075, open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The mailing address is Mail Station 5140, 600 N. Robert St., St. Paul, MN 55146. Probate questions go to the county court system instead.

Minnesota evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law.

What the official sources say

  • An eviction action begins by filing a complaint describing the premises and the facts authorizing recovery of possession. (Minn. Stat. 504B.321; source)
  • The court issues a summons with an appearance date not less than seven nor more than 14 days from issuance (subject to subd. 2). (Minn. Stat. 504B.321; source)
  • Eviction grounds include holding over after foreclosure redemption expires, after lease expiration, or after rent becomes due under the lease. (Minn. Stat. 504B.285; source)
  • After foreclosure redemption expires, a tenant under a lease beginning after the mortgage date and before expiration must get at least 90 days' written notice to vacate if the tenant pays rent and follows the lease. (Minn. Stat. 504B.285 subd. 1a; source)
  • If a bona fide lease runs more than 90 days past redemption expiration, the successor must allow occupancy to the lease end with 90 days' written notice, except if the successor or a buyer will occupy as primary residence. (Minn. Stat. 504B.285 subd. 1a(b); source)
  • Seller disclosure requirements do not apply to a transfer to a tenant in possession. (Minn. Stat. 513.54; source)

What are the steps of a Minnesota eviction case?

A landlord files a complaint in district court, the court issues a summons for a hearing, the tenant answers at that appearance, and a judge or jury decides the case. If the landlord wins, the court enters judgment for possession and issues a writ of recovery of premises and order to vacate. The rules sit in Minn. Stat. 504B.321 and the sections around it in chapter 504B.

The complaint must name the person being sued (with a date of birth when known), describe the premises, state the facts that justify taking possession, and ask for possession. Attachments depend on the claim:

  • The current written lease and any addenda.
  • An itemized accounting when the claim is unpaid rent.
  • For a lease breach, the clause relied on, the conduct, and the dates.
  • Any notice to vacate or notice to quit, when holding over is the claim.
  • A statement of whether Section 8, tax credit, or another subsidy program covers the tenancy, with the administering agency named.

The Judicial Branch publishes form HOU102, the Eviction Complaint, and lets landlords build forms through Minnesota Guide and File, which can allow electronic filing in some cases. A Self-Help Center at the Minnesota Judicial Center, Room G25, 25 Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., St. Paul, helps people without a lawyer.

How does a Minnesota tenant have to be served?

The summons and complaint must reach the tenant at least seven days before the court date, by one of the methods in Minn. Stat. 504B.332. That section was added in 2024 and replaced the older section 504B.331, which the legislature repealed.

The default method is service the way a civil summons is served in district court. When the tenant cannot be found in the county, the papers can be left with a person of suitable age at the last usual home. If those fail, the landlord can mail the papers and post them on the unit door, but only after at least two personal service attempts on different days, one of them between 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. An affidavit of service is due at least three days before the hearing.

A landlord who regularly texts or emails the tenant must also send a time-stamped message with the hearing date, time, and place at least seven days ahead. If the tenant does not appear, the trial goes ahead without them.

What happens at a Minnesota eviction hearing and trial?

At the appearance named in the summons the tenant may answer, and the court then sets a trial date that allows a fair and timely decision, taking account of complexity, discovery, witnesses, and the chance to find a lawyer (Minn. Stat. 504B.335). Either side may demand a jury, and the case otherwise runs like other civil actions.

Courts may not make a tenant pay money into court, post a bond, or pay the landlord directly before the case ends. The one exception is a case likely to last more than ten days, where the court may order security capped at the periodic rent that accrues while the case is pending, with nothing for amounts owed before the filing date.

Two types of case move faster. A complaint under section 504B.171 (drugs, prostitution, unlawful firearms, stolen property) or one alleging serious danger to other residents or intentional serious damage can get an expedited hearing five to seven days after the summons issues, with service inside 24 hours. A landlord who asks for expedited handling without enough basis can face a civil penalty of up to $500.

How fast can a Minnesota tenant be removed after judgment?

After a ruling for the landlord, the court tells the sheriff or another officer to remove the tenant, usually after a stay of up to seven days. Each stage has its own clock.

StageTimingStatute

Source: Minnesota Statutes chapter 504B. A tenant who says they will appeal gets a stay of the writ for at least 24 hours, and if they stay in the home during the appeal the bond covers only regular rent as it comes due, never back rent or late fees. If the landlord holds the tenant's belongings, the landlord must prepare a signed, dated inventory with the officer present and mail a copy to the tenant.

Can a Minnesota tenant stop an eviction by paying?

For a nonpayment case, yes, until possession is delivered. Under Minn. Stat. 504B.291 the tenant can redeem the tenancy by paying the rent in arrears with interest, the costs of the action, and an attorney's fee that cannot exceed $5, and by keeping the other lease promises. A written guarantee of funds from a government agency or a tax-exempt group that runs a rental assistance program can stand in for cash.

Redemption is unavailable when the landlord also alleges a material lease violation. The statute also says a partial payment taken before the writ issues counts toward the balance without ending the case only if both sides agreed to that in writing. Once a landlord gets possession, a certified copy of the judgment is recorded with the county recorder, or the registrar of titles for registered land.

What does an eviction mean when a landlord wants to sell the rented house?

A tenant living in a house that is up for sale can be removed only through the court steps above, and several Minnesota rules shape what a buyer inherits.

  • Foreclosure: a tenant whose lease began after the mortgage date and before redemption ended must get at least 90 days' written notice to vacate from the new owner, and a bona fide lease running longer can last to its end (Minn. Stat. 504B.285, subd. 1a).
  • Deposits: when a landlord's interest ends by sale, the deposit and interest must be passed to the buyer or returned to the tenant within 60 days, and the buyer can limit its duty to the stated amount if the tenant does not object within 20 days (Minn. Stat. 504B.178, subds. 5 and 6).
  • Disclosure: the seller disclosure rules do not apply to a transfer to a tenant in possession (Minn. Stat. 513.54).
  • No self-help: forcing a tenant out or removing belongings outside the court process is unlawful ouster under section 504B.365, subd. 5.

The records side matters too. An eviction file is closed to the public until final judgment, and a case dismissed for defective filing or service is expunged under 504B.321. Check the county recorder for any recorded judgment before closing.

More questions about Minnesota Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Minnesota eviction take from filing to move-out?

The statutes set no single total. The first hearing falls 7 to 14 days after the summons issues, the court then picks a trial date based on the case, and a stay of up to seven days follows a judgment for the landlord. An appeal or a redemption payment can change the timeline.

Can a Minnesota landlord change the locks or remove a tenant's belongings?

No. Section 504B.281 bars taking possession by force, and section 504B.365 limits removal to the officer executing the court's order. A landlord who removes belongings outside that process commits an unlawful ouster unless the premises were abandoned.

How long does a tenant have to appeal an eviction judgment in Minnesota?

Fifteen days, following the civil appeal rules for district court. Telling the court of the intent to appeal brings a stay of the writ for at least 24 hours, and a tenant who remains in the home posts a bond for regular rent only.

Is a Minnesota eviction case a public record?

Not until the court enters a final judgment. Before that, only the parties and licensed attorneys helping them can see the file. A case the tenant wins, or one dismissed for a defective filing, is expunged.

What happens to a tenant's deposit when the landlord sells?

Within 60 days of the sale the landlord must transfer the deposit with interest to the buyer and notify the tenant, or return it to the tenant. The buyer takes the landlord's rights and duties over the deposit under Minn. Stat. 504B.178.

A Minnesota deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • Statutory short-form quitclaim deed: grantor 'conveys and quitclaims' to grantee 'all interest' in the described real estate. (Minn. Stat. 507.07; source)
  • A duly executed quitclaim conveys all right, title and interest of the grantor but does not extend to after-acquired title unless words expressing that intention are added. (Minn. Stat. 507.07; source)
  • Quitclaim deeds with consideration over $3,000 require a certificate of real estate value. (Minn. Stat. 272.115; source)
  • County recorder fee for indexing and recording any deed or other instrument is $46. (Minn. Stat. 357.18; source)
  • Recorded documents must be on sheets no larger than 8.5 x 14 inches, black ink, not smaller than 8-point type, on white paper of at least 20-pound weight. (Minn. Stat. 507.093; source)
  • First page must have a three-inch blank space at the top and half-inch borders on each side and bottom. (Minn. Stat. 507.093; source)

What does a Minnesota quitclaim deed actually transfer?

It transfers whatever interest the signer holds in the described property and nothing more. Under Minn. Stat. 507.07, the statutory form has the grantor say the deed "conveys and quitclaims" to the grantee "all interest" in the real estate, which is why owners reach for it when they want to move their own share without promising anything about the title.

The same section spells out the limits. A properly executed quitclaim carries the grantor's right, title and interest at the time of signing, but it does not reach title the grantor acquires later unless the deed adds words showing that intent. A warranty deed in the same statute is different: it brings covenants that the grantor holds the property in fee simple, has the right to convey it, that it is free of encumbrances, that the grantee will have quiet possession, and that the grantor will defend the title. A quitclaim carries none of those promises.

For a Minnesota homeowner, that means a quitclaim fits transfers where everyone already knows the history of the property, such as adding or removing a family member. When you sell to an outside buyer, expect the buyer, the lender or the title company to say which deed they need before closing.

What does the deed have to look like before a county recorder will take it?

It must be legible, signed in ink by the parties, and acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer. Minn. Stat. 507.24 requires that an instrument affecting real estate be legible and archivable, executed and acknowledged, with the acknowledgment certified. Paper documents must carry the original signatures of the parties and of the notary. A deed can be recorded in every county where any of the land lies.

Page layout is set by Minn. Stat. 507.093. The main points:

  • Sheets no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, in black ink, in type no smaller than 8 point.
  • White paper of at least 20-pound weight, with no background color or images.
  • On page one, a blank space measuring three inches from the top, with a half-inch border on each side and the bottom. The right half is reserved for recording information and the left half for tax certification.
  • The document title displayed prominently below that blank space, or on an attached administrative page.
  • No added sheet that covers any printed part of the form.

Recorders have some give. Minn. Stat. 357.18, subdivision 5, says a document should meet these standards but should not be rejected unless it is illegible or cannot be archived. That rule covers documents dated after July 31, 1997.

What will the recorder charge for filing a Minnesota quitclaim deed?

The statutory fee for indexing and recording a deed is $46. Section 357.18, subdivision 1, caps county recorder charges at that amount for any deed or other instrument and divides it three ways: $10.50 to the state general fund, $10 to the recorder's technology fund, and $25.50 to the county general fund. A certified copy of a recorded record costs $10.

The recording fee is only one of the charges that can arrive with a deed. The table below shows how the main Minnesota requirements line up, with the statute that sets each one.

Charges and filings tied to a Minnesota quitclaim deed
ItemRuleStatute
Recording fee$46 per deed or instrument357.18 subd. 1
Certificate of real estate valueRequired when the price is over $3,000272.115 subd. 1
State deed tax$1.65 at $3,000 or less; .0033 of net consideration above that287.21 subd. 1
Auditor's tax checkAuditor notes "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered"272.12

Source pages: the certificate of value statute, the deed tax statute and the tax-paid-before-recording statute.

When does a quitclaim deed need a certificate of real estate value?

Any time the property is sold for more than $3,000. Minn. Stat. 272.115 applies whether the sale is made by warranty deed, quitclaim deed, contract for deed or any other method. The grantor, the grantee or their legal agent files the certificate with the auditor of the county in which the land lies, at the time the deed is presented for recording.

Value for a deed that is not a gift is the full actual consideration, paid or still to be paid, including any lien the buyer assumes. Personal property sold with the house is listed and subtracted from the price. The form asks for the property's classification, any planned change in use, the financing terms, and the Social Security number or federal employer identification number of each grantor and grantee. Those numbers are private data, though the statute lets them go to the commissioner of revenue for tax administration.

A spouse who is not an owner of record and signs only to release a marital interest is not counted as a grantor for the number requirement. The statute gives sample wording for the deed that lets the auditor accept the certificate without that spouse's number.

  • No certificate is needed for a conveyance to the state or a political subdivision for road right-of-way when the agency has agreed to file a list with the commissioner of revenue.
  • None is needed for a designated transfer that is labeled as one on the first page or signature page.
  • None is needed for a deed that carries out a recorded contract for deed and refers to it by document number or book and page.

Does a quitclaim deed trigger Minnesota deed tax?

Sometimes. Minn. Stat. 287.21 taxes each deed that conveys Minnesota real property. When there is no consideration, or the consideration is $3,000 or less (not counting liens left on the property), the tax is $1.65. Above $3,000 the tax is .0033 of the net consideration, so a sale with $200,000 of net consideration owes $660. It is due when the deed is presented for recording.

Section 287.22 lists transfers the tax does not apply to. Several matter to families:

  • A deed of distribution by a personal representative.
  • A deed to or from a co-owner that partitions an undivided interest in the same property.
  • A decree of marriage dissolution, or a deed or instrument between the parties that follows the decree.
  • A transfer on death deed under section 507.071, and any affidavit that refers to it.
  • A deed or instrument that grants, creates, modifies or ends an easement.

A quitclaim to a relative for no payment falls in the no-consideration bracket and owes the $1.65 minimum, while a deed that carries out a divorce decree is on the exempt list.

Why does the county auditor look at the deed first?

The auditor confirms that no taxes are delinquent before the recorder will accept it. Under Minn. Stat. 272.12, when a deed is presented for transfer the auditor checks the records for delinquent taxes or a tax sale. If taxes are owed, the auditor certifies that, and the transfer is entered after they are paid. If none are owed, the auditor writes "no delinquent taxes and transfer entered" on the instrument over an official signature. Without that statement the recorder or registrar of titles must refuse the deed.

The statute lists instruments that can be recorded without the certificate, among them deeds of distribution by a personal representative, transfer on death deeds, decrees and judgments. Ordinary deeds between living owners are not on that list.

What happens to the homestead classification after a deed is recorded?

It ends for the next assessment year unless the new owner applies. Subdivision 3 of section 272.115 directs the assessor to remove the homestead classification from sold or transferred property for the following assessment year, unless the grantee completes a homestead application under section 273.124, subdivision 13, and qualifies.

That application goes to the county assessor, and section 273.124 says that if none has been filed by December 31, the assessor classifies the property as nonhomestead for taxes payable the next year. Subdivision 4 adds that property sold or transferred with a required certificate of value cannot be classified as homestead until the certificate has been filed. A person receiving a house by quitclaim should file the homestead application as soon as they move in, since a missed filing leaves the property classified as nonhomestead for that year.

Can a quitclaim deed be used when you sell the house?

The law allows it, since section 272.115 names quitclaim deeds among the methods of sale. The practical question is what the buyer will accept. Because a quitclaim carries no covenants, a buyer who wants a promise of clear title will usually ask for something stronger and will order a title search either way.

Ask the recorder's office there what it needs, and talk to a Minnesota real estate attorney or title company about the form. The Morrison County Recorder's Office, for one, states on its website that it cannot give legal advice or prepare legal documents and points people to a real estate attorney or an abstract or title company.

More questions about Minnesota Quitclaim Deed

Does Minnesota recognize a quitclaim deed?

Yes. Minn. Stat. 507.07 provides the form, and a deed that is signed, acknowledged and recorded passes the grantor's interest to the grantee. It passes only the interest the grantor actually holds when signing.

What fee applies when a quitclaim deed is filed in Minnesota?

The recording fee is $46 under Minn. Stat. 357.18. Add the $1.65 minimum deed tax for transfers with no price or a price of $3,000 or less, or .0033 of net consideration above that, unless the transfer is exempt under section 287.22.

Does a Minnesota quitclaim deed remove a name from the mortgage?

Not by itself. The deed addresses who holds title to the real estate, while the loan is a separate agreement with the lender. Ask the lender and a Minnesota attorney how the transfer affects the loan before you sign.

Must a Minnesota quitclaim deed be notarized?

Yes. Minn. Stat. 507.24 requires the deed to be acknowledged and the acknowledgment certified, and paper deeds must carry the original signatures of the parties and the notary.

Who files a certificate of real estate value?

The grantor, the grantee or the legal agent of either files it with the county auditor when the deed is presented for recording, if the property sold for more than $3,000. Minn. Stat. 272.115 sets that rule.

What the official sources say

  • A TOD deed is valid if recorded in a county where part of the property lies before the grantor owner's death. (Minn. Stat. 507.071; source)
  • No county auditor certification or certificate of real estate value is required when a TOD deed is recorded. (Minn. Stat. 507.071; source)

  • TOD deeds are exempt from state deed tax. (Minn. Stat. 287.22(15); source)

  • A personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate real property, including the homestead, without consent of devisees or heirs unless specifically devised, but the homestead cannot be sold if the spouse takes an interest without the spouse's written consent. (Minn. Stat. 524.3-715(23); source)

Minnesota Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Minnesota rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Minnesota?

It is a recorded deed that hands real estate to a named beneficiary when the owner dies, without a probate sale in between. Minn. Stat. 507.071 says the deed must state that it is effective only on the death of one or more of the grantor owners. Until that death, the deed has no effect on title, so the owner keeps full control of the house.

The statute does give the beneficiary one right during the owner's life: an insurable interest, so the beneficiary can insure the property against loss that happens after the transfer takes effect. The deed must still follow every rule that applies to Minnesota deeds in general, including those in sections 507.02, 507.24 and 507.34.

If a spouse who is neither a grantor owner nor an owner signs the deed or consents to it in writing, that joinder is conclusive proof the spouse gives up any marital interest in the property once the transfer takes effect.

What makes a Minnesota transfer on death deed valid?

The deed has to be recorded before the owner dies. Subdivision 8 of section 507.071 makes a transfer on death deed valid only if it is recorded in a county where at least part of the described property sits, and recorded before the death of the grantor owner on whose death the transfer depends. A deed signed but sitting in a drawer does nothing.

  • No notice to the beneficiary, no consent from the beneficiary and no delivery of the deed to the beneficiary is required while the owner is alive (subd. 18).
  • An attorney-in-fact can sign the deed if the power of attorney gives authority to execute deeds (subd. 7).
  • The deed can name a trust, a trustee or another entity that can legally hold title (subd. 9).
  • The deed can name several beneficiaries and successor beneficiaries, and can state the condition under which a successor takes (subds. 4 and 5).
  • The statute includes a sample form that begins "Transfer on Death Deed" and lets the owner choose between effective on the death of the last grantor and effective on the death of a named one (subd. 24).

When the deed is presented for recording, the county auditor does not certify taxes or ownership transfer, and no certificate of real estate value is required.

Can an owner still sell or revoke after recording one?

Yes to both. A transfer on death deed can be revoked at any time by the grantor owner, or by any one of several grantor owners. Under subdivision 10, a revocation cancels the whole deed and takes effect only if it is recorded in a county where part of the property lies before the death of the owner who signed it. The statute prints a short form of revocation in subdivision 25.

Selling does not need the beneficiary's permission. If the owner later conveys all or part of the property to someone else by a deed that is not a transfer on death deed, the transfer on death deed becomes ineffective as to the interest that was sold. It stays effective for any other interest the owner still holds at death.

Two further rules prevent surprises:

  • A will does not revoke a recorded transfer on death deed (subd. 19).
  • If an owner records more than one such deed for the same property, the one with the latest acknowledgment date, recorded before death, controls and the earlier ones are void, except for land the later deed leaves out (subd. 13).

Which situations change who actually inherits?

Joint ownership, a beneficiary who dies first, and property bought after signing each change the result. The table pulls the main cases from section 507.071 into one place.

How section 507.071 handles common complications
SituationResult under the statuteSubdivision
Joint tenants all sign a deedTransfer happens only after the last surviving owner dies; if that owner did not sign, the deed is void6
Beneficiary dies before the ownerIf the beneficiary is a grandparent or descendant of a grandparent of the owner, that person's surviving issue take in place unless a successor is named11
Every beneficiary fails to surviveNo transfer; the deed is void12
Owner no longer owns the property at deathDeed is void as to that part; beneficiary has rights to unpaid sale, condemnation or insurance proceeds14
Property acquired after signingNot covered unless the deed says so in specific language21

A beneficiary who is a grandparent or a descendant of a grandparent of the owner is covered by the antilapse rule in subdivision 11, so that person's surviving issue can step in. Words such as "if he or she survives me" count as a clear survivorship condition.

What does the beneficiary record after the owner dies?

The beneficiary records an affidavit of identity and survivorship with a certified record of death, and a clearance certificate for public assistance claims. Subdivision 20 allows the affidavit and the certificate to be combined and recorded together or separately in each county where the land lies. The affidavit must include the name and mailing address of the person who should receive future property tax statements.

The clearance certificate comes from the county agency that recovers medical assistance benefits from estates. Under subdivision 23, anyone claiming an interest, or their attorney, applies to that agency in the county where the property is located, listing the legal description of each parcel. Subdivision 3 says the beneficiary must record the certificate in every county in which the described land lies.

This step matters to anyone planning to sell the inherited house, because registered property cannot get a new certificate of title until the clearance certificate is recorded. A person with an interest can also ask the district court for an order allowing a sale free of a public assistance claim or lien, with the proceeds handled as section 525.313 provides.

What debts and claims stay with the property?

Everything that was attached on the date of death stays attached. Subdivision 3 says the beneficiary takes the interest subject to existing conveyances, contracts, mortgages, liens, judgments, tax liens and similar encumbrances, including the claim of a surviving spouse who did not join in the deed. Subdivision 15 adds that a mortgage passes with the property and the owner's will cannot require the estate to pay it off first.

State and county medical assistance claims are the notable exception to the idea that this deed avoids the estate. If other estate assets do not cover such a claim, the beneficiary must account for it, but liability is limited to the value of the interest received. Interests of beneficiaries cannot be sold, pledged or reached by their creditors before the owner dies, according to subdivision 22.

Is there deed tax or an auditor's stamp on these deeds?

No on both. Minn. Stat. 287.22, clause 15, exempts a transfer on death deed, and any affidavit that refers to one, from the state deed tax. A deed of distribution by a personal representative is exempt too. Section 272.12 lists transfer on death deeds among the instruments that can be recorded without the county auditor's "no delinquent taxes" note. You still pay the county recorder's regular recording fee, which section 357.18 sets at $46 for a deed.

Where do you start if you are selling a house tied to one of these deeds?

Start by working out who holds title today. While the owner is living, the owner still holds it and can sign a sale deed. After death, the beneficiary has to complete the recording steps above, then the house can be listed or sold to a cash buyer like any other property.

Call the county recorder where the property sits to ask what they have on file and what they will need to record the affidavit. For the legal questions, such as a disputed survivorship or a claim against the estate, talk to a Minnesota probate attorney. District court handles disputes, and subdivision 26 sends matters in counties with a probate division to that division.

More questions about Minnesota Transfer on Death Deed

Does a transfer on death deed avoid probate in Minnesota?

The covered property passes under the recorded deed when the owner dies, and a will does not undo it. Under Minn. Stat. 507.071 the beneficiary then records an affidavit and a clearance certificate, and claims by the state or county can still reach the property.

Can I change my mind after recording a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Any grantor owner can revoke the deed at any time by recording a revocation in a county where part of the property lies before that owner dies.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. Subdivision 18 says no signature, consent, notice or delivery to the beneficiary is required during the owner's lifetime.

Is a transfer on death deed subject to Minnesota deed tax?

No. Minn. Stat. 287.22 exempts transfer on death deeds, and affidavits that refer to them, from the state deed tax.

What happens if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

If a grandparent or descendant of a grandparent of the owner is the beneficiary, that person's surviving issue take in place unless the deed names a successor. If no beneficiary or successor survives, no transfer occurs and the deed is void.

What the official sources say

  • Small estate affidavit (personal property): 30 days after death, a successor may collect personal property by affidavit if the entire probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $75,000 and no personal representative application is pending. (Minn. Stat. 524.3-1201; source)
  • A personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate real property, including the homestead, without consent of devisees or heirs unless specifically devised, but the homestead cannot be sold if the spouse takes an interest without the spouse's written consent. (Minn. Stat. 524.3-715(23); source)
  • A deed of distribution by a personal representative is exempt from state deed tax. (Minn. Stat. 287.22; source)
  • Seller disclosure requirements do not apply to a transfer to heirs or devisees of a decedent. (Minn. Stat. 513.54; source)

How does probate work in Minnesota?

Chapter 524 of the Minnesota statutes governs estates. Most families begin with an informal case, where a court registrar acts on a sworn application and no hearing is held. A judge gets involved in a formal case, which is the track for objections and for contested wills. Whichever track applies, the person appointed personal representative gathers the assets, pays what is owed and hands the rest to those entitled.

The registrar may issue a statement of informal probate once 120 hours have gone by since the death (Minn. Stat. 524.3-302). Until a formal order says otherwise, that informal probate binds everyone. The application itself must give the applicant's connection to the estate, the decedent's name, birthdate, death date and home county, and every known spouse, child, heir and devisee, per Minn. Stat. 524.3-301.

Waiting too long closes the door. Under Minn. Stat. 524.3-108, an informal or formal proceeding generally cannot start after three years have passed from the death. Someone challenging a will that was informally probated has until the later of 12 months after that probate or three years after the death.

Who can serve as personal representative of a Minnesota estate?

The priority order in Minn. Stat. 524.3-203 begins with whoever a probated will names. A surviving spouse who also inherits comes next, then other devisees, then the spouse alone, then other heirs. A creditor may apply once 45 days have gone by, and a conservator who was never discharged may apply after 90 days.

A spouse, devisee or heir in that ranking can pass the role to a qualified nominee. Any adult may give up the right in a signed writing filed with the court. Only a formal proceeding can hear an objection to an appointment, and if an heir with a real stake objects, the court can choose someone acceptable to the people holding over half the likely distributable value.

Can a Minnesota estate avoid probate?

Small ones can. A successor who waits 30 days after the death may present an affidavit to collect personal property when the whole probate estate, counted on the day of death and net of liens, comes to $75,000 or less and nobody has applied for a personal representative (Minn. Stat. 524.3-1201). Banks, safe deposit companies and people holding the property must then turn it over on a certified death record plus the affidavit, and the motor vehicle registrar can issue a new title the same way.

Another shortcut is the summary proceeding in Minn. Stat. 524.3-1203. A court can find that the decedent left nothing, or only exempt property and sums owed for the property selection, family allowances and certain costs, and then assign what exists to the right people without full administration.

  • Count only the probate estate against the $75,000 figure.
  • Have a real estate attorney or title examiner confirm whether the house sits in the probate estate at all, because a deed that takes effect on death or shared ownership can change the answer.
  • Call the probate clerk of the decedent's home county and request the forms that fit your situation.

The affidavit route is written for personal property, so a house in the estate needs a different path.

Can the personal representative sell an inherited Minnesota house?

Generally yes. Clause 23 of Minn. Stat. 524.3-715 lets the representative sell, mortgage or lease estate land, homestead included, on cash or credit terms and without asking the heirs, unless the will gave that property to a named person. A surviving spouse who takes an interest in the homestead must sign a written consent first.

Who inherits the homestead is settled by Minn. Stat. 524.2-402. A spouse with no descendants to share with takes it outright. When descendants survive, the spouse keeps a life interest and the descendants split the remainder. If it lands with a spouse or descendants, creditors without a charge on it at death cannot reach it, except for the state hospital and medical assistance claims.

Heirs who do not want to keep a house can list it with a broker, take an as-is cash offer, or carry it until the court closes the estate. The representative's powers also reach repairs, insurance, and paying taxes and reasonable costs of administration out of estate funds.

What are the key Minnesota probate deadlines?

The table gathers the periods that control when an estate closes and when a sale can finish with clean title.

Minnesota probate time limits, with statute source
EventPeriodSource
Informal probate statementNot before 120 hours have passedMinn. Stat. 524.3-302
Affidavit for a small estateAfter 30 days, with $75,000 or less at stakeMinn. Stat. 524.3-1201
Claims after newspaper noticeFour monthsMinn. Stat. 524.3-801, 524.3-803
Mailing to known creditorsThree months from first publicationMinn. Stat. 524.3-801
Final cutoff for pre-death claimsOne year from the deathMinn. Stat. 524.3-803
Inventory of the estateLater of six months from appointment or nine months from deathMinn. Stat. 524.3-706
Sworn statement to closeFour months or more after appointmentMinn. Stat. 524.3-1003
Outer limit to open a caseThree yearsMinn. Stat. 524.3-108

How are creditors handled in a Minnesota probate?

Once a general personal representative is appointed, the court administrator arranges publication of a notice in a county legal newspaper, run weekly for two weeks. Creditors then have four months to present claims. The representative separately serves known, identified creditors within three months of the first publication. Minn. Stat. 524.3-801 counts a creditor as known when someone told the representative of the claim, when accessible financial records disclose it, or when a diligent search of those records would turn it up.

Section Minn. Stat. 524.3-803 bars claims that arose before death unless they arrive in time. Newspaper-only creditors get four months from the published notice. A served creditor gets the later of four months from first publication or one month after service. Regardless of notice, one year from death is the outer boundary, although state medical assistance and similar benefit recovery claims survive past it. Liens on estate property can still be enforced.

What taxes and paperwork apply when selling an inherited Minnesota home?

No state deed tax is due on a deed of distribution signed by a personal representative (Minn. Stat. 287.22). That deed still goes to the county auditor, who records the transfer in the office books and notes "transfer entered" on it under Minn. Stat. 272.12. A deed to an outside buyer faces an extra check: the auditor looks for delinquent taxes, and the recorder will not accept the deed without the auditor's notation. Any delinquent property tax therefore has to be paid before the deed can be recorded.

Seller disclosure duties in sections 513.52 to 513.60 carry an exception for transfers to heirs or devisees of a decedent (Minn. Stat. 513.54). A sale above $3,000 also requires a certificate of value filed with the auditor as the deed goes in for recording (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

Before the closing date, line up these items:

  • a payoff figure for any delinquent property tax on the parcel;
  • the certificate of value for the county auditor;
  • the auditor's transfer notation on the recorded deed;
  • a written answer from the Minnesota Department of Revenue or the estate's attorney on whether an estate tax return is needed for an estate of this size.

More questions about Minnesota Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Is probate required before an heir can sell a Minnesota house?

If the house is titled in the decedent's name alone, yes: it is part of the estate, and the personal representative signs the sale documents. A very small estate can use an affidavit for personal property, and a house that never belonged to the probate estate needs no representative.

What counts as a small estate in Minnesota?

One worth $75,000 or less on the day of death, wherever the assets sit, after liens and encumbrances. Thirty days must pass after the death, and no petition to appoint a personal representative can be on file.

When do creditors lose the right to claim against a Minnesota estate?

Four months after the published notice, or one month after service when that is later, and no later than one year after the death for debts that arose earlier. Claims arising at or after death follow their own four-month periods.

Is there a cutoff for opening a Minnesota probate case?

Yes, three years after the death for most cases. A special administrator can still be appointed afterward for limited jobs such as collecting assets.

Do heirs owe deed tax when the estate deeds them a house?

No. A deed of distribution from a personal representative appears on the list of deeds exempt from state deed tax. The county auditor still processes it before the recorder takes it.

This guide covers what official sources say about Minnesota tax on a house sale.

What the official sources say

  • Minnesota DOR lists individual income tax rates of 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85%. (Income Tax Rates and Brackets | Minnesota Department of Revenue; source)

Does Minnesota tax a gain on a house sale?

Yes, when the gain is not wiped out by the federal home sale exclusion. The Department of Revenue's 2026 bracket announcement lists four income tax rates, 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85%, and it has no separate schedule for capital gains.

A good share of Minnesota sellers owe nothing on a main home. Section 121 of the Internal Revenue Code shelters the first $250,000 of profit, or $500,000 for a married couple filing together, and the state's net investment income schedule leaves out any profit that is excluded for regular tax. Owners of rentals, second homes or recently bought houses face more steps. The sections below start with Minnesota's rates and add-on tax, then walk through the federal tests that decide how much gain is left.

What are the Minnesota income tax rates for a sale in 2026?

These brackets cover tax year 2026, with returns filed in 2027. Indexing moved the thresholds up 2.369% from 2025 and left the rates alone. Married separate brackets are half of the joint ones.

2026 Minnesota income tax brackets (Minnesota Department of Revenue, December 16, 2025)
RateSingleMarried joint
5.35%Up to $33,310Up to $48,700
6.80%$33,311 to $109,430$48,701 to $193,480
7.85%$109,431 to $203,150$193,481 to $337,930
9.85%$203,151 and over$337,931 and over

The department also posts head of household and married separate brackets. Its 2026 standard deductions are $15,300 for single and married separate filers, $30,600 for married joint and $23,000 for head of household. These thresholds apply to taxable income, so a large gain in the year of sale can push the top slice of your income into the 9.85% bracket.

Who pays the extra 1% Minnesota net investment income tax?

Minnesota layers a 1% tax on net investment income over $1,000,000 for individuals, estates and trusts. On Schedule NIIT you subtract $1,000,000 from Minnesota net investment income and multiply what remains by 0.01. Corporations do not file it.

The schedule names capital gains alongside interest, dividends, rent, royalties and non-qualified annuities. Three details matter to someone selling a house:

  • Profit that is excluded from gross income for regular tax, like the main home shelter, never becomes net investment income.
  • Net gain on Minnesota class 2a agricultural land is subtracted out of the state calculation.
  • Estimated payment rules apply as they do to other individual tax, so an owner expecting a very large gain should raise withholding or estimates to avoid an underpayment penalty.

Partners and shareholders covered by a composite or pass-through entity tax still attach Schedule NIIT to Form M1 once investment income passes $1 million.

How much of my Minnesota home gain can I exclude?

The shelter is $250,000 per seller or $500,000 on a joint return, and the department's schedule applies it to the state net investment tax too. Two tests must be passed. The owner, or one spouse, must have held title for 24 months inside the five years before closing. Both spouses must have used the house as their residence for 24 months inside that same span. Those months can be spread out, and the two tests may be met in different two-year stretches.

The IRS generally denies the shelter to a seller who already used it on another house during the prior two years. Extended-duty members of the uniformed services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community may pause the five-year clock for up to a decade.

Here is a simple case. A single seller with a $310,000 profit on a qualifying main home shelters $250,000 and reports $60,000. A married couple filing jointly with the same profit reports none of it.

What federal rules decide the size of my taxable gain?

Gain equals the amount realized minus adjusted basis. Basis usually starts with what you paid. Houses that were inherited or given to you follow other rules in IRS Publication 551, and a loss on a personal residence cannot be deducted. Owning for over a year makes the gain long-term. A year or less makes it short-term, and short-term gain is taxed at ordinary graduated rates.

The table on IRS Topic 409 is for 2025, and for most filers it caps the long-term rate at 15%.

  • 0% on 2025 taxable income to $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for married joint and $64,750 for head of household.
  • 15% above those lines, up to $533,400 single, $600,050 joint or $566,700 head of household.
  • 20% on whatever sits above the 15% band.
  • Up to 25% on unrecaptured section 1250 gain, which comes into play for a rental where depreciation was taken.

A rental or other investment property sold at a loss is treated differently from a personal home. Net capital losses reduce other income by no more than $3,000 a year, or $1,500 for married filing separately, and the rest carries forward. A taxable gain can also require quarterly estimated payments to the IRS and to Minnesota, so run the numbers before closing. Look up the IRS figures for a 2026 closing before you estimate. Report on Form 8949 and Schedule D. A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on the return even when the entire profit is sheltered. If the buyer pays over several years the installment method is available, and the shelter still applies.

How does Minnesota tax a nonresident who sells Minnesota property?

For people who live elsewhere, Minnesota Statutes 290.17, subdivision 2 assigns income and gains from tangible property in the state to Minnesota when the owner does not use the property in a business. Residents are different: the statute says resident individuals' income is not allocated outside the state, so a resident reports the whole gain here.

An out-of-state owner who sells a Minnesota house, cabin or lot should expect a Minnesota return for the year of sale. For the net investment tax, part-year residents and nonresidents allocate the figure using Schedule M1NR lines 1 through 8. If you moved out of Minnesota before closing, the date of the move can change the filing, so call the Department of Revenue before you sign the closing statement.

What did Minnesota change about capital gains over time?

Until the 1987 reform, Minnesota let taxpayers leave 60% of capital gains out of taxable income, and they could also subtract federal income tax. The department lists that change as one of several that broadened the tax base. The top rate in the department's historical explanation is 9.85%, and brackets have been indexed for inflation since 1979. The department notes that average tax paid can be far lower than the top rate: a married couple with $400,000 of total income in its 2014 example owes about 6.0% of that income, even though its last dollar is taxed at 9.85%.

Keep the closing disclosure, the records of what you paid, and receipts for improvements, because those papers fix your basis.

More questions about Minnesota Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

What is the Minnesota capital gains tax rate in 2026?

Minnesota has no separate capital gains rate in its 2026 bracket announcement. Taxable gain is taxed within the 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85% income tax brackets. A 1% net investment income tax applies only above $1,000,000.

Is there Minnesota tax on a main home that qualifies for the federal shelter?

Not on the sheltered part. Minnesota's net investment schedule leaves excluded gain out, and profit above the cap is taxable income.

How many months of residence does the home sale shelter require?

Twenty-four months of ownership and twenty-four months of use, both inside the five years before closing. The two periods can be different stretches.

Does the Minnesota net investment income tax apply to all home sales?

No. It applies only above $1,000,000 of Minnesota net investment income and skips gain that is excluded for regular income tax. The tax equals 1% of the excess.

Must I report a sale if the 1099-S shows a gain I can exclude?

Yes. IRS Topic 701 says a 1099-S triggers reporting even when all of the gain can be excluded, on Form 8949 and Schedule D when those are required.
